utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The Trial Chamber apologises for coming in late. Apparently some messages were sent through to some of the Judges that we were starting a bit late. I asked that the witness be not brought in because there is just one urgent matter that we need to deal with. I don't like doing this in between -- during the testimony of a witness, but the Trial Chamber had hoped to do this yesterday. There wasn't any time, and I think it should be done now. This is in relation to the Defence motion for protective measures for Witness MM-117. Shall we -- does this need private session? Yes, it does. May we move into private session, please? Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Once again, I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I've moved over here not to confuse you or to make you turn further, but just because I thought I might have better luck with the computer. When we broke yesterday we were talking about events in Saborsko on the 5th of August, 1991. And at the beginning of the cross-examination yesterday you agreed that by the summer of 1991 there were Serb forces, meaning police, TO, and JNA units, in both Plaski and Plitvice on both sides of the villages of Saborsko, Vukovici, and Poljanak. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that in August 1991 in Saborsko there were only some members of the Croatian police or MUP, correct, in terms of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that at that time on the Croatian side all men who were fit to serve in the military were armed, just as on the Serbian side, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But in terms of organised forces, units, there were some policemen in Saborsko, and that's it; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was involved in some kind of military organisation. They had units that were called people's defence or national defence. They were armed and most likely paid for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on what basis do you say they were most likely paid? Is that just speculation on your part or do you have information on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information from talking to people who were captured and who said that from Slunj money would arrive regularly to Saborsko for salaries. That means that before any operations were conducted in Saborsko, they had established MUP, reserve forces of MUP, and units of people's defence. This is what was written on the emblem that they wore. There was that infamous chequer-board and the text "people's defence" on the emblem. I know that for a fact because I brought one such souvenir home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're contending that in August of 1991 the -- all of the men in Saborsko were organised into units? That's your contention?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were definitely armed. As for their internal organisation, I can't testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, we testified about the targeting of Saborsko that occurred on the 5th of August, 1991. And I will put to you that in fact before August of -- the 5th of August, 1991, and on the 5th of August, 1991, there were no attacks from Saborsko and nobody in Saborsko had done anything to be -- had done anything to deserve being called or labelled an Ustasha. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- you've answered the question. And I put to you also that Serb forces targeted Saborsko starting on the 5th of August, 1991, and every day -- nearly every day after that not because of provocations, as you claim, but because Saborsko was in the way and the Serb forces wanted to drive the people out of Saborsko and wanted to link up Plaski with the rest of the SAO Krajina. Isn't that right, sir? And you can answer that yes or no. I don't need explanation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at the end -- at the end of August, 1991, the shelling of Poljanak also began almost on a daily basis. Is that -- do you know anything about that? Can you comment on that either way? Because yesterday you indicated that you don't know about Poljanak or Plitvice. So are you able to comment on whether shelling also began in Poljanak at the end of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August of 1991, the Serbian Territorial Defence from Plaski had only 82-millimetre mortars. Such mortars could not reach the village of Poljanak from our positions --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because I think you misunderstood my question. I was not suggesting that Poljanak was being shelled by forces in Plaski. I was merely suggesting -- I was merely putting to you that Poljanak was shelled by Serb forces starting at the end of August 1991. Do you know anything about that, sir, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were so far away from Poljanak that I wasn't even able to hear that. I didn't hear any detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move into September of 1991. And you testified in your direct examination that some men arrived in Saborsko in September of 1991, and you said that they were -- there were about 200 men and that they armed everybody in Saborsko. Now, first of all, in fact there were only about a hundred men who came in September of 1991. Isn't that true, sir, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the first part of your question, based on my information there were 200 of them. I wasn't able to count them, even though I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you -- you testified in your direct examination that they armed everybody in Saborsko, but you have said just a moment ago that everybody was already armed in Saborsko in August of 1991. Are you able to reconcile those to statements that you've made?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and in a very simple way. I said that they armed Saborsko with heavy weaponry, and then I told you how many mortars and recoilless guns they brought in. They needed crew of several people to service that kind of weaponry. As for August, people at that time were armed, mostly with Kalashnikov, which are considered infantry weapons. If necessary, I will repeat what kind of weapons arrived at that time, based on my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. But in your direct examination, it's at page 8983, you testified that: "They brought infantry weapons for all the remaining population in Saborsko."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought in weaponry. Now, whether I said that that applied to the remaining population, I can't remember. I accept that I might have said that. At any rate --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So which is it? Did the population have -- were they armed with the infantry weapons in August or did -- were they armed in September? You've now given two different versions, so I'll give you a chance to choose which one you want to go with.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the activists of the Croatian Democratic Union in Saborsko were armed back in late 1990, as is the case in the entire state of Croatia. The first unit that arrived there, this special unit from Ogulin, established --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because I just really want an answer to my question. Did -- was the population in Saborsko armed with infantry weapons in August of 1991 or only after the men arrived in September of 1991? Which one, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were armed in August, that somebody brought weapons to them in August, no. They had been in possession of weapons in late 1990, especially when the check-point was established between the 30th and 31st of March, 1991. Following that, weapons were brought in from many sources. And as for the 25th of September, the remaining population received it. And if somebody had just a hunting rifle, then they received also automatic or semi-automatic rifles too. As I said, everybody was armed, everybody who was fit for military service, as was the case on our side too. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm not sure that you've answered my question, but I think the transcript speaks for itself, and I'll just leave it there and move on in the interests of time. You testified, and this is at 8983 of the transcript, that the arrival of these reinforcements, whether it's a hundred or 200, as you say, in September 1991 "ruined the negotiations that were going on." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, on your own account, on your own account between the dates of the 31st of March, 1991, and September of 1991, you have told us that the following things happened in Plaski, among other things: A special-purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police was created; it was trained in Golubic; it received weapons there. The Croat police left Plaski because they wouldn't sign the loyalty oath that they were required to sign to the SAO Krajina. The Serb TO was established in Plaski, and it was armed by the JNA. Now, why don't you say any of those things ruined the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In everything that you enumerated you said the Serbian Territorial Defence in Plaski. It wasn't called that, and there was some members who were Croats, Croats from Plaski. We felt threatened to a much greater extent from Josipdol than from Saborsko, Josipdol and Ogulin, and it suited us to find a peaceful resolution. There were too few of us to establish a circular defence, and we were cut off from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you could, please, focus on my question. You indicated that the fact that reinforcements arrived in Saborsko in September 1991 caused a break-down in the negotiations between -- what you claimed were negotiations between Plaski and Saborsko. My question is: Why wasn't arming and organisation that was occurring on the side of -- your side in Plaski, why didn't -- why don't you say that they also caused or that even more so caused break-down in negotiations? Are you able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to give you the Croatian perspective or my perspective in Saborski? I'm telling you that it suited us to find a peaceful settlement in Saborsko and we tried everything. Up until that time, no residents in Saborsko were killed and there were instances of exchange of fire, but nothing serious. This was like that until the end of September. There was still good chances for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I tell you something, Witness. You've just been reminded before you testified this afternoon to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth, not a Croatian perspective or a Serbian perspective. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you have been telling us a Serbian perspective all this time and not the truth, please do tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, I'll ask you to talk to the accused not to make such silly noises in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do that. I myself didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard something. Have you been telling us a Serbian perspective during your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we may continue. Mr. Martic considered one question to be a leading one, and he waved his head, but he won't do that in the future. Should he have any other comments, he will pass me a note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, waved his head?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't see a waving of the head by Mr. Martic, I heard something, a noise, number one. Number two, I'm not quite sure what a leading question could that have been. The witness is being asked questions -- was being asked questions by the Bench. But anyway, I accept what you say ear saying that he says it will not recur. Judge Nosworthy wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, I wish to inquiry with the other members of the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of my testimony I gave a solemn declaration, and I'm still abiding by it. As for the events, I'm just testifying about the events about which I have personal knowledge and in which I participated. As for this question, I took it that the Prosecutor was requiring me to speculate, as was the case several times in the past. They're asking me to give my assumptions. I can't give you any assumptions now. I can only give you information about my position at the time 15 years ago when I was part of authorities. I can just give you what I know, and then you can draw your own conclusions. I can't change the way things happen, nor do I wish to mislead anybody and make them believe that things happened in a different way. No, I'm just telling you about the events in which I participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now -- sorry, just a second. Now, if the Prosecutor is asking you to speculate, all you need to say to him is: Sorry, I will be speculating if I answer that question and I'd rather not speculate. You don't go on to say: Are you asking me to give you the Croatian perspective or my perspective in Saborski? Okay? Which is what you said -- at least that's what was translated to us in the English. Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, I never want you to speculate or to guess. Please just tell me what you know; and if you don't know the answer, just tell me you don't know. Now, I'm going to try to rephrase the question I put to you concerning the negotiations, the so-called negotiations, because you -- it's your testimony that they broke down because these reinforcements arrived in Saborsko. Was it your view at that time that on your side, that is the Serb side, in Plaski you had a right to arm yourselves and organise yourselves and train and create formations, but the Serbs in -- I mean the Croats in Saborsko did not have that right? And that's why you say that the negotiations broke down when they had reinforcements brought in in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, there is several questions in one question. It's not clear to me. What are you referring to? Are you asking me whether they had the right to arm themselves? Is that the question? I apologise, but it's just not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. And you've done the right thing. If it's not clear to you, then just tell me. I guess my question is: Why do you say that the negotiations broke down when reinforcements arrived in Saborsko? Why did that cause negotiations to break down?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reinforcements that arrived in Saborsko on their way to Saborsko in Glibodolski Kriz, they captured our guards, several policemen, several civilians, and the late Major Milan Boca. They also cut off the road where I was. By some chance they didn't capture me personally. These people that they captured and taken to Saborsko were beaten and mistreated. After these people were exchanged for some Croats that we captured on the following night, it was impossible to recognise Milan Boca. He personally told me who beat him, how, and why. As for the prisoners from Saborsko who were captured by us, they were not mistreated, absolutely not. And once the blood is shed, then it is very difficult to, once again, re-establish negotiations. It takes a lot of years for that to happen. This man was beaten only because he was a JNA major in retirement and because they link him to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact the men who were arrested on your side were Vlado Vukovic, Ivica Vukovic, and Nijaz Poric. Those were the men you're referring to who were captured from Saborsko and arrested on your side; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have to give you a more detailed answer. These three people you mentioned remained on our side after the exchange, because they were captured after the exchange. And before them there were three or four men who had been captured for nine of our people. This was an all-for-all exchange. As for this group of people who had been sent to cut off the road between Slunj and Saborsko, they captured the three men that you mentioned and they were brought to Plaski on the evening of the day when the exchange had taken place in Licka Jesenica. I remember that I thought it unusual that the third gentleman was not from Saborsko; he was a Muslim by ethnicity. And I kept wondering how come he was in Saborsko at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with respect to Vlado Vukovic, he was detained at the Plaski police station for approximately 12 days, he was beaten by Martic's police, and he -- you, in fact, you yourself beat him with a belt. Isn't that true, sir? You're smiling.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I heard just now is not in good taste. I never beat any prisoner. That evening when Vlado Vukovic arrived and the other two men, the man who captured him was called Drago Jovanovic, and he invited him to his birthday and -- to his birthday party. And they wanted to release them after that. And I said: We will not release them. We will take them to Korenica because there are other captured Serbs. This Vlado Vukovic attended the birthday party and sat at the table and ate together with other invitees. They had gone to Slunj earlier, several days earlier, to attend another birthday party. It was not a mission, no. They went to a birthday party. And this is the truth about Vlado Vukovic. He likes to play the role of a victim --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he -- I'm just explaining to you how come he's giving false testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just limit yourself -- please not comment on his testimony. Just provide your own testimony, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just at that point, would he still have been in detention at the birthday parties? It seems somewhat strange and curious. Was he attended by persons who were keeping him in detention or what was the nature of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a bit of a strange case, but it's true. They were not tied. We did not have a prison in Plaski. We just had a small police station, and the facility was very small. There was an area behind the stairs that they used as detention, and there was no -- no proper detention facility. I saw Vlado Vukovic that first night, and then he was transferred to some other police force. I don't think that he spent 12 days there. I know that he was transferred to Korenica soon thereafter, and I don't know what happened to him afterwards, probably the same thing that happened to other prisoners. As for Plaski, that evening I didn't beat him. I talked to him and I especially talked to the Muslim gentleman, because I was particularly interested in learning how many other people like them there were. They said that they had arrived from Karlovac and other places, and then I asked him how come there were any Muslims in Saborsko. And he said that his wife was from there originally and that he had come to defend his father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. But at the birthday party or parties, he could not just have walked away from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was still our prisoner. But I told you, just to explain, that there was no mistreatment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand, I just want to get -- do I understand you to be saying, sir, that you -- you - when I say "you," I mean your unit there - attended parties with people that they had arrested or you just allowed him to go alone to a party and then come back? What happened? He's detained, then he goes to a party; I don't understand this. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were brought to the police station in Plaski. We interviewed them. They were arrested by three people who had spent three days in the forest. That was my order, because we needed prisoners were exchange, and I told my men: Don't come back without prisoners. We had some of our people in Croatian prisons, and they came back after the exchange was completed. So they came to the police station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just come to the party issue. While you had them arrested, you went to parties with them? That's just what I want to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. That's exactly how it was. The man who captured them is called Dragomir Dokmanovic, and he took them to his house. It was a small type of house. He took them there. He was there together with his friends and the prisoners, and after the party he took them back for the night to the police station. They were not tied. There was no mistreatment whatsoever. His house is some 500 to 600 metres from the police station. This is why I felt so bad when I read the transcript from the Milosevic trial in which he accused the residents of Plaski for mistreating him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Milosevic trial. We're here in the Martic trial now, okay? We're dealing with the Martic trial. Now, I think -- am I right to say that earlier you also mentioned that these very detainees went to Slunj? I don't know whether it was for a party also there, but I think you mentioned Slunj. So it's not -- they didn't just go -- yeah. Can you answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Between Saborsko, which was under Croat -- Croatian control, and Slunj, which was also under the Croatian control, there's a road. It was along that road that they were on their way to Slunj, and it was along that road that they were taken prisoner. They were then taken to Plaski across a forest track. I can even show it to you on a map, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, just listen to my question and answer my question. Did these people also go to Slunj while they were in detention in Plaski, yes or no? Just don't tell me things that I'm not asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they were taken prisoner as they were coming back from Saborsko to Slunj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting, you may proceed. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it in fact the case that the reason Vlado Vukovic was taken to that party, if that in fact happened, was it was to show him off as a prisoner, to taunt him, to ridicule him, to parade him? Isn't that in fact what happened, whether in that party or at some other location on that first day. That's what happened, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. We wanted to show them that because they had surrendered without putting up resistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were just being nice to them to take them to the party. Is that the end of the sentence? You were rewarding them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have the feeling now that I'm being ridiculed myself here. I'm not sure, Your Honour, if I should respond to such a provocation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I was -- I was not trying to ridicule you in any way. I was simply trying to finish your -- what I thought would be the end of your sentence. You said: "We wanted to show them that because they had surrendered without putting up resistance," and I assumed you were going to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the words uttered by the Prosecutor just now amount to his explanation. However, the witness himself was interrupted by the Prosecutor as he was trying to give an answer to a very precise and difficult question, which was why they treated a prisoner this way. He was interrupted in giving his answer and was then given the comment that he was given. Perhaps an intervention from the Bench is not warranted, but nevertheless the Prosecutor should treat the witness fairly as a witness should be treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I always try to treat witnesses fairly, and I'm trying to treat this witness as fairly as all others. I did -- it's true, I did interrupt the witness because I was trying -- I'm trying to move on, I'm trying to get through this material. When I saw the first half of the sentence, I thought it might be interesting to have the end, and I thought I knew and so I put it to him. If he disagrees, that's the end of the sentence, he can just tell me. He can just tell me what the end of the sentence was going to be. I'm not trying to create any unfairness or anything here. So I'm happy to just ask him what the end of the sentence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you said we wanted to show -- you took them to the party. "We wanted to show them that because they surrendered without putting up resistance." And what were you going to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that because they cooperated during the interview by providing us accurate and complete information as to who arrived in Saborsko and with what sorts of weaponry, they were not mistreated at all and they were clearly told that they were taken prisoner only with a view to being exchanged and that this was the sole purpose of their capture and that they would be exchanged as soon as possible. I didn't take them to the party. I told you that Dragomir Dokmanovic, also known as Zuja, took them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer you've just provided us really had nothing to do with the reason they were taken to the party; correct? You're talking about something else here, about why they were taken prisoner and the exchange.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that they were taken to the birthday party as a reward for the fact that they did not cause us any trouble and for the fact that they cooperated with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go back to these negotiations that you described. The demand on your side was that the Croats in Saborsko simply disarmed themselves. You testified that you demanded that the Croats surrender their weapons to the JNA, and then that -- that was your demand in the negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions the Serbs were called upon to surrender JNA weapons, which they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in Plaski the -- you told us yesterday that the TO in Plaski was armed by the Serbs in July of 1991 and that the special-purpose unit had been armed. You weren't about -- you weren't going to turn over those weapons, were you? You were simply asking the Croat side to disarm itself.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in your question - at least this is how it was interpreted to me - you said that the TO in Plaski was armed by the Serbs. What does this mean? Which Serbs do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, you're absolutely right. That is exactly what I said and I misspoke. What I meant to say was armed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the JNA is superior to the TO, and the most senior JNA officer is the one who decides who will be mobilised and with what means and when. This was in 1991 when there was the JNA and the TO in Yugoslavia. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, by September of 1991 the JNA was openly siding with the Serbs in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to tell me whether you're referring to the period prior to September or as of September. Which month do you have in mind and which year? You have to put a precise question to me because you seem to be putting words into my mouth. I'm listening very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: By September 1991. Exactly what you're asking for; that's what's contained in the question. The month and the year are given there. What more do you want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd say that the case was rather as of September, after the attack by the Croatian forces on the JNA barracks. I believe it was in the month of September that the first JNA barracks fell under the attack of the Croatian forces. As I said, the first one fell in Vukovar, I don't remember the date, but I do remember it was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say that was in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly in October. I don't know the exact date, but I'm sure that it took place in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But in fact, already on August 26th of 1991, the JNA and the TO and Martic's police, the Serb TO under the authority of the SAO Krajina and Martic's police engaged in a joint military operation in Kijevo. Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, sir. All the information I have I learned subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't know anything about it, that's fine. I'll really move on. Now, let's -- you told -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What does that mean, "I don't know anything about that. All the information I have I learned subsequently"? You were asked what you know by today, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, when did you learn information about Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know where Kijevo was. I had never been in the area or even close to Kijevo in my life. I only knew what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, please listen to the question. You told us that: "All the information I have learned subsequently." When did you learn that information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt the information when it was broadcast by the Croatian television, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What date, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was still available to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that, what date did you learn that? At the time, in August/September 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that exactly, sir. You're asking me things that happened is a years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please approach the microphones. You cannot be heard by the people who are supposed to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you can't remember the exact date -- I mean, did you learn it at the time, during 1991, or is this something that you learned later?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was fighting in Kijevo, and I heard it on Croatia television probably at the time the operation took place. However, I still do not have reliable information as to who took part in the operation or the details of it. I heard on television that Kijevo fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay. If you don't have reliable information as to who took part, that was my question and I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the question was: When did you hear this information said. But as to who took part was never part of the question. When did you hear of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably at the time the events happened, because the Croatian television broadcast the information on the events as soon as they happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact the information didn't come to you subsequently; it came to you contemporaneously. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to tell me which piece of information you're referring to exactly. I heard, as everybody else did, that Kijevo fell. I did not listen to what the Croatian propaganda had to say because they referred to us as the Serb Chetniks and the Serb Chetnik armada --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you stop there. You have not been talking Chetniks. And don't ask me what information -- you're talking about the information that you said came to you subsequently. You talked about getting information subsequently, and I'm saying to you, therefore, that information didn't come to you subsequently. It came to you contemporaneously with the events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his question, Mr. Prosecutor stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Consider my question, sir. Forget about Mr. Prosecutor's questions. I'm talking to you about my question. Did the information come to you contemporaneously or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information concerning the fall of Kijevo was something I received or heard on Croatian television. I did not have either the time to watch Croatian television or the electricity most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, earlier today you told us that you did not know about events in Poljanak in August of 1991. Does that remain true for September, October, November of 1991, that you do not know anything about what happened in Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I -- I know nothing of Poljanak. I categorically state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine. Then I won't put any questions to you about that. Let's move to November of 1991. At the beginning of November of 1991, do you -- are you aware that there were some people in Saborsko who were killed by Serb fire on the -- around the 1st of November, 1991? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk now about the events leading up to the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991. First of all, you were asked about the relative -- in your direct examination, the Defence attorney asked you about the relative strength of the forces in Saborsko in November of 1991, as compared to the forces of the JNA and Plaski -- Plaski units. Now, even accepting that there were 400 fighters in Saborsko, accepting that for a moment, with artillery weapons, you would agree with me that the JNA, the TO, and the police of the SAO Krajina surrounding Saborsko had overwhelming force compared to that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not agree with that. I can state the exact make-up of units. I know that for a fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that Tactical Group 2 included an armoured battalion, mixed artillery division, a light infantry division, and that's just the Tactical Group 2, that's not even talking about the 5th Partisan Brigade, the TO, the police. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was interpreted to me as the light infantry artillery battalion. I tell you that this cannot exist at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if there's a document which says that Tactical Group 2 included that, you would -- your evidence would be that that document is wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Apparently there is a comma missing, so to say, in what was interpreted to the witness. The question was: Isn't it true that Tactical Group 2 included an armoured battalion, mixed artillery division, a light infantry division," --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand. Yes, thank you, Your Honour, I had missed that. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is that clear now to you, Witness? You understand the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you have as the mixed artillery unit is the mixed artillery battalion because a division should have several brigades on its strength, at least based on my knowledge of the establishment. So at least it should have some 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers. Can you tell me -- or can anyone tell me exactly whether these forces were there? I should have known about them, given that I had lived in the area. Because an artillery battalion, "divizion," would have several batteries and several artillery pieces. A division is quite a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it then your answer that the Tactical Group 2 did not include these things that I have stated?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You confused me with -- by mentioning the light infantry division. That's something I never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be of assistance, and I'd rather not do that under the heading of an objection. If we look at the document referring to Tactical Group 2, there are acronyms there, and these acronyms in the B/C/S could be interpreted as a division. However, when one looks at all at abbreviations together, MAD is short for the mixed artillery battalion, which only has several batteries on its strength. One of the units which formed part of Tactical Group 2 was a reconnaissance detachment. If the unit indeed had been a division, this particular unit should at least have been on the strength of a company. The question put by the Prosecutor is impossible, both in terms of the military doctrine and linguistically. But I don't want to testify here. Perhaps the Prosecutor should invite the witness to explain what the abbreviations stand for in this document rather than offering an interpretation of them, if you agree, Your Honours. As things stand at the moment, we have a confusion caused which is difficult to clear up later on. I'm saying this because I am aware of the fact that my learned friend may be inadvertently causing confusion. However, as I myself served in the military, as did the witness, I know what these abbreviations stand for and can fully understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic, for trying to clear up and without testifying, but also thank you for your testimony. I think the confusion between the Prosecution and the witness is really no confusion. The witness heard what was interpreted to him as "light infantry artillery." Now, Mr. Whiting had never said anything of the sort, and -- just a second, please. Just a second. Mr. Whiting had heard nothing -- had said nothing of the sort, and that is why Judge Hoepfel tried to draw the attention of both Mr. Whiting and the witness to what Mr. Whiting had said so that the witness could answer. And if you look at what the witness -- what Mr. Whiting had said - I'm trying to get it - it was -- there was absolutely no statement to the effect that there was anything like light infantry -- 24.7. Now, Mr. Whiting said: "Sir, isn't it true that Tactical Group 2 included an armoured battalion, mixed artillery division, a light infantry division, and that's just the Tactical Group 2. That's not even talking about the 5th Partisan Brigade, the TO, the police. Would you agree with that, sir?" If there's something wrong with that, then I'm sure the witness can clear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, I do think the witness is disputing that it was the strength of a division, is my understanding of his evidence. So perhaps I'll give him an opportunity to further explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's just go through it. Why don't you tell us what your understanding is of what comprised the Tactical Group 2, what forces were comprising Tactical Group 2, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully submit that you misunderstood me. It was -- what I heard was "light infantry division" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, it's not going to be productive to go over this. Just -- I think we can solve this if you just tell us what you knew.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please place these abbreviations on the overhead projector here and then I can interpret them. Because "light infantry division" is something I never heard of in all my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to put the question differently. I want you to tell us what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you know -- what do you say was comprised in the Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't the commander of Tactical Group 2. This information was presented to me here. I do not want to speculate --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer is you don't know. You don't know what forces were in Tactical Group 2. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for a fact there was no light infantry division in there and I categorically assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from that, are you able to tell us at all what units comprised Tactical Group 2, yes or no? If you can't tell us, that's fine, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me try to approach this in a -- in a more basic way. You would agree with me, would you not, that the Serb forces in November of 1991 had tanks, air support, long-range artillery, APCs, all things that those 400 men, even assuming that there are 400 men, in Saborsko did not have. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you because these were not Serb forces. This was the JNA. I know for a fact that the commanders of some of these units were Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, let's put aside that issue, whether the JNA was -- constituted Serb forces because you would agree with me, right, that the JNA participated in the attack on Saborsko along with the TO and the police, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I raise an objection regardless of what sort of an answer the witness would have. On the basis of what can the Prosecutor state that the JNA equipment amounts to Serb equipment or equipment of the Serb forces? These are very important material, legal matters, relevant for the entire case against Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting, the witness objected also before, Mr. Whiting, to the use of the word "Serb," and you suggested that he put it aside, that issue. I think let's try to be as accurate as we possibly can. What you are referring to is the JNA, TO, SAO Krajina TO, and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. But of course, Your Honour, it's our case that -- it's the Prosecution case that the JNA was acting with the Serb forces and constituted part of the Serb forces, but that's not the issue that I want to take up with the witness right now. And Your Honour is absolutely correct that I should be more distinct about it for that -- the purposes of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, for purposes of the question, and for purposes of your case we know where Serbs and Croats fall in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Put aside the -- whether the JNA is Serb forces or not. You would agree with me that the JNA, the TO -- the forces that attacked Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, had at their disposal tanks, air support, long-range artillery, and APCs, all things that the Croats in Saborsko did not have. Will you agree or disagree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander of that operation who decided on the use of forces. I can't comment that because I would have attacked Saborsko with much fewer forces because I would have been afraid of counter-attack from Ogulin. However, Cedomir Bulat was the commander, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, that's an answer to a different question than the one I asked. I asked whether the forces that attacked Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, had at their disposal tanks, air support, long-range artillery, and APCs, all things that the Croats in Saborsko did not have. You agree with that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, you answered instead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you to answer, would you agree with me. Do you agree or disagree with what I have said in, and you're free to answer how you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Agree or disagree --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- in those terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was superiority on the side of the Yugoslav People's Army because they were on the offensive, and those who are on the offensive have to be more powerful than those who are defending themselves. That's how it is in all the armies in the world and all the wars that have been waged in the world. Everything else would be adventure-like on the part of those attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on that note?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just would ask that it be noted on the record that the witness is refusing to answer the question, or has not answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to pursue it when we come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that note, we will break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try and see if we can get this issue resolved one last time. In -- during the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, the JNA had air support, tanks, long-range artillery, APCs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Croats in Saborsko did not have these things; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, they had some weapons. I told you which ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They did not have tanks, air support, long-range artillery, and APCs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You are very accurate on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look, please, if we could at Exhibit 52. You've seen this exhibit before in your direct examination. And you testified, did you not, that this was an order for the attack on Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, there we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to be clear, it's dated the 7th of November, 1991, at the top there, top left; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in the first paragraph it talks about Ustasha formations in Saborsko, right? Do you see that? It says 400 --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And further down, if we go down, scroll down a little bit, it says there -- thank you. You'll see that it says in those points that have dashes the following fire points have been noticed so far in Borik it says there are 50 Ustashas, in north-west from Alan there's a group of 200 Ustashas. In Saborsko, 150 Ustashas. Do you see that in the document, in this military order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So this order is saying that there are approximately 400 fighters in Saborsko and the surrounding hamlets of Saborsko and that they're all Ustashas; correct? Is that how you understand this order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified on Monday that when the reinforcements arrived in September of 1991 to Saborsko, that there was celebrating and cheering by the people. So in your mind at least, the people were supporting -- the people of Saborsko were supporting these Ustashas; correct? Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. I wasn't present in Saborsko at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting, didn't we have a debate before in the first session about the people in Saborsko or -- who had weapons being no Ustashas? And you are now putting in the mouth of the witness the word "Ustashas." That's a little bit -- to me it seems a little fast -- we can go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a reference to a debate we had yesterday in reference to an exhibit, which was -- I think it's Exhibit 38. And it was whether -- as I recall the debate, it was whether the reference to Ustashas was to fighters in Saborsko or residents. And here I'm only going on -- I'm only asking questions based on this document that is before the witness, and the reference to Ustashas -- 400 Ustashas is in the document, Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 4, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of today's transcript, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. But I think the witness said that, no, you are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we just check. Yeah, okay. It was not confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Nobody deserved being called Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But it was still not the opposite expressed, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it was -- the opposite was expressed yesterday, Your Honour. The witness did testify about it yesterday on this very -- very point, at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I had in mind what was discussed today, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you -- do you recall testifying on Monday that when the reinforcements arrived in September of 1991 to Saborsko there was celebrating by the people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they fired in the air because I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact, referring to the fighters in Saborsko as Ustashas, as this order does on the 7th of November, 1991, serves only the purpose of demonising those men. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you. They were demonised enough by their own deeds. Colonel Djordjevic wrote this order; I didn't. And I don't know what the purpose was of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But -- well, you know that the purpose was to order the attack on Saborsko. You agree with that, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an order, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, the people in Saborsko, the men in Saborsko had done nothing to deserve being called Ustashas. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir. I've already spoken about that. In Saborsko at the time there was still living Ustashas, those who had been Ustashas in the World War II and who had participated in combat as members of German units. And it stayed a tradition in certain families and they bragged about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, if anybody had been participating in activities in World War II, they certainly would have been quite old by 1991, right? At least 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were old, that's right, even though there was some people who were younger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this reference to 400 Ustashas in Saborsko in this order is not -- that's not a reference to 400, 70-year-old men, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I stated clearly that every armed Croat who represented a real threat to the security of Serbs was an Ustasha in my eyes, and I believe that the same opinion was shared by the person who signed this order. That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- generally an accepted claim at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, the term "Ustasha" means more than that. That's a reference to a state in World War II that didn't -- that wasn't just in conflict with the Serbs, but that in your -- in your view and the view of many people committed crimes against Serb civilians, including even genocide; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you used that term in 1991 to refer to somebody, you're not just referring to somebody who's in conflict with the Serbs -- with the JNA or with the Serb military, you're using that to refer to somebody who threatens Serb civilians, who threatens the Serb people in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the forces that were in Saborsko at the time clearly wrote the letter U, which was a symbol of Ustashas during World War II. This letter was written in many locations in Saborsko. I also saw this letter on their uniforms, on their caps and hats. I didn't call them that. This is how they bragged. They considered themselves to be the followers, direct followers, of Ustashas from World War II. And if Colonel Djordjevic called them that at the time, then I share his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're claiming that the men in -- these 400 men in Saborsko were dressed in uniforms with the U symbol on them. Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, but there were some with U symbols that they had preserved in their houses from the time of World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me, would you not, that among any group, particularly in a war -- and that kind of conflict, there are going to be individual extremists, whether it be on the Croat side or on the Serb side. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. On the Serb side we never had people who were as extreme as Ustashas were, both in World War II and in the latest war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I won't debate you on that point at this moment, and actually we're not here to debate, but I -- let's focus on the Croat side. Whether there were a few individual extremists, even in Saborsko, there were not 400 Ustasha followers in Saborsko, were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with you. Why didn't they isolate them and why didn't they send them back to where they had come from if they had conflicts with them? By your leave, let me say this. On the other side behind Ogulin were Serb villages that were in the similar situation as Saborsko. They had received weapons, and they surrendered them to Croats because they didn't have any chances of winning, and I drew a parallel between them and the people in Saborsko. Why didn't people in Saborsko expel such men as Luka Hodak and some others? No, they let themselves become victims, which means that the Ustasha ideology was the dominant one at the time in Saborsko. That's the real truth, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, you believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I doubt that you're going to get the witness to budge. He has his own view --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate it. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: With respect, my belief is that we have spent enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: He has a position, he's maintaining his position, whether right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this order dated the 7th of November, 1991, was issued before anybody knew about those three men that you say were killed at Glibodol cross; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that they were killed on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you testified on Monday that -- this is at 8992 of the transcript that: "Before the order was issued," meaning the order to attack Saborsko was issued, "a terrible incident took place at Glibodol cross." That was wrong, right? That was incorrect what you said on that -- in that testimony, because now you've told us that it happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the order that I received as a company commander was after the event. This order here is the order -- if you can bring it to the beginning, I think you'll see that it was sent to the Operations Group 3, command of the 13th Corps, forward command post, and it was sent to the command of Tactical Group 2. And only upon receiving this did the Tactical Group 2 send the order further to the battalion commander, and then he sent it down to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and in addition to this crime --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please complete my answer because that's not all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I am focussed on this at the moment, sir. On Monday, when you testified, you knew that this order, that the original order to attack Saborsko had been given before the event occurred at Glibodol cross. You knew that on Monday when you testified, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know back in 1991 that there would be an attack on Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about on Monday. When you testified on Monday that before the order was issued a terrible incident took place at Glibodol cross. You knew on Monday that in fact the order to attack Saborsko had been issued before the terrible incident at Glibodol cross; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon, what do you mean by issued before this attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Written or delivered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I understood the -- I understood that before the decision was made that -- because that was sort of the import of the testimony. That's how I had understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is more precise now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew, sir, on Monday that before the decision -- that the decision to attack Saborsko was made before the incident at Glibodol cross, right? You knew that on Monday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm testifying here about the facts that I knew at the time in November before the attack, and I'm saying about what was known to all of the fighters in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is very simple. Just don't try to evade the question. The question is: On Monday, when you started testifying here in this trial, did you know then that this decision to attack had been made before the incident at Glibodol cross? You should -- you should be able to answer to that question. Did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will very clearly state that I learned that once I saw this document, and back then in 1991 I learned that after the incident. Here I saw it when I saw the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you. Will you please answer the question. Did you know on Monday when you testified or didn't you know? It is a very simple question. It doesn't need a lot of explanation. You should be able to say: Yes, I knew; or no, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember when this document was shown to me for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question. That's not the question. The question to you simply is: Do you -- did you know on Monday when you had testified that when this decision was made it was before the incident that took place at Glibodol cross? You either did or you did not know. Just tell us that, sir. What's so difficult about that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Monday I learned that this was written on the 7th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not being asked when you learnt. I'm just asking you a question. On Monday when you testified, did you know that at the time the decision was made the incident had Glibodol had not taken place yet? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I was asked before I was shown this document. I saw this document for the first time here. I wasn't paying attention to the date, and I can see now here that in the upper right-hand corner it says when it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I can't allow you to go on telling me things that have nothing to do with my question. My question is very simple to you. Whether you saw this document on Monday for the first time or not, it's immaterial. And whether you did look at the date on Monday or not, it's immaterial. I might remind you, though, that counsel for the Defence drew your attention to this date on Monday. But that's not the point. The point is on Monday when you testified, did you know that the incident at Glibodol bridge took place after this decision was made? And I'm sure you can answer that very simply. Yes, I knew, or no, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I learned about that here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not asking you about when you learnt. Did you know that this decision had been taken before the incident at Glibodol. Just answer that question. Don't phrase your own question and answer the question that you put to yourself; answer the question that's put to you by whoever is questioning you. Did you know? And if you don't want to answer, fine, then we'll record that you're evading questions, if that's what you are doing. We'll record that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My answer to your question is: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it didn't have to take you that long to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look at the map, and if we could have page -- Exhibit 23, page 19, and the last four digits of the ERN is 6288. It is the atlas, Your Honour. And if we could zoom in again around Ogulin, which is right in the middle there. Now -- if you could just scroll down a little bit. And there do you see Glibodol there? It's in the lower half --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could zoom in just a little bit on Glibodol. It's the Glibodol Licka -- right there, exactly. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that Glibodol cross is at the -- is at the point where the road from Glibodol meets the road from Dabar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And actually, if you wouldn't mind marking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could give the witness a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you could mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've drawn a circle, a red circle. Is that -- have you drawn a red circle around Glibodol cross?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this is evident on the map, but that -- Glibodol cross is on the other side of Licka Jesenica from Saborsko; correct? There's Glibodol cross, then Licka Jesenica, and then you reach Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Then you reach --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't agree with you on geographic issues either. There is a direct road from Glibodolski Kriz to Saborsko which is not shown on this map. If you have a military map, and I believe you do, then you will be able to clearly see that here. This map is not large enough, and not all of the roads are shown there. One doesn't need to go via indirect roads. There is a direct road leading through Lugovi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which goes above the barracks in Licka Jesenica. Towards the railway station in Tovarnik [as interpreted], there's a road there leading directly to Saborsko. So going from Glibodolski Kriz to Saborsko, one doesn't necessarily have to go to Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine. Now, nonetheless, you would agree with me that the MUP forces that attacked at Glibodol cross in November of 1991 on -- around the 8th of November, 1991, were in fact from the other side of -- not from the Saborsko side but were from the -- from Ogulin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's not correct. This was a joint attack that commenced on the 4th and not on the 8th. I testified about that when Mr. Milovancevic showed me an official note that was compiled by TG 2 or I don't know who, and there you have the date of the commencement of the action and of the place from where the action was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And what happened starting -- I believe it was actually on the 5th of November, not on the 4th, but in any event it's not document. What happened is there was an attack on Licka Jesenica from both sides, from the Glibodol side, from MUP forces on the Glibodol side, and also from forces in Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. On that occasion the forces from Saborsko killed Branko Vukelic, Sapina, the medical nurse, Javorka Vukelic, and Dusanka Grba was seriously wounded. I believe it very important to note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, wasn't it your testimony that the forces in Saborsko were directing fire but that the fire was actually coming from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent, yes. I agree with you this time. However, Branko Vukelic was killed at the threshold of his home; whereas Nurse Vukelic was killed at the entrance to the health centre, which was clearly marked with a red cross. And I believe the attack was launched from the village of Lipice facing Glibodol. However, one cannot see the barracks clearly from Plaski. One can see it from Saborsko. And I'm talking about the Vidakovic mount where the health centre was housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this attack that started on the 5th of November, 1991, its objective was the barracks, the JNA barracks at Licka Jesenica; correct? That's what was being attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the objective of the attack was, but I know that the barracks at Licka Jesenica was the most sought-after target. It was hit with more than 200 projectiles and shells, and I know that it -- the infantry forces approached the barracks from two sides. I've already spoken about this. If you want me to, I can tell you some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I think that's fine. But just to be clear, this attack, as you say, was on two sides. There was forces from Ogulin or from the Ogulin side that was in Glibodol and there were the men in Saborsko, and from both sides they attacked Licka Jesenica; correct? And I think you've explained that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This time I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me then, sir, that the men -- those three men who were killed on November 8th, 1991, at Glibodol cross, they would have been killed then by MUP forces from Ogulin, not anybody from Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be grateful to you if you told me exactly who killed them, if we could uncover that. This was a coordinated action --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let me put it this way -- let's take it a different way. It's not known who killed them exactly; correct? Nobody knows who killed them; is that right? Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrator knows and the eye-witnesses do. This was a show put on for all the soldiers there, and it lasted for several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine, fine. Aside from the perpetrators and any witnesses, you don't know - you don't know, sir - do you, as you sit here today, who killed them; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we focus, however, on what units or forces were operating in that area, would you agree with me that the likelihood is, it's most, if not certain, that forces from Ogulin were the ones involved in that event on the 8th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
