utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Could my learned friend specify which forces he's referring to from Ogulin. Whose side is involved? There are two sides, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't think that -- I didn't think there was any mystery about that. I'm talking about Croat forces, the Croat MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Croat -- the MUP -- the Croatian MUP forces from Ogulin were operating around Glibodol. They're the ones most likely to be involved in this event, right, and not the people from Saborsko? Right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. This was coordinated action, and the entire area of Kapela was under their control. And the people from Saborsko could freely come to Glibodol. You're asking me to speculate, and this is something I cannot do. I cannot give you an accurate answer to that question, although I'd very much like to know who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it fair to say, then, that you have no idea whether people from Saborsko were actually involved in the murder of those three men. Is that fair to say? You don't know if it was people from Saborsko or people from somewhere else; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some information to the effect that persons from Saborsko took part in that crime. The information I have is not reliable because it's second-hand information. This is not my personal experience, although I do consider the information accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, when you say it's not reliable, I assume you mean it's -- if it's not reliable that you would not want to take an important -- make an important decision based on that information, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to say that, because I am testifying here under an oath about the matters that I personally experienced and acted upon. And it is for this reason only that I do not wish to speak on this matter. I do not want it to be put down on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood. I'm not going to ask you to speak on it. All I'm asking you is that you would not base an important decision on unreliable information, would you, sir? If you had an important decision to make, you would not base it on unreliable information. This is not a trick question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an easy person to entrap. I'm listening carefully and giving you truthful answers. In my parts, you say that the person who is a thief is equally to blame as the one who is on the lookout for him to be involved in a theft. Now, if you're asking me whether it's the men from Saborsko or from Ogulin, I can tell you that I heard people boasting about having taken part in that action, and they were from Saborsko. I heard them over a radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you told us that you thought that was unreliable information, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that this was hearsay, this was second-hand information. I didn't personally see that. And had I seen it, I would have made sure that I found the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said, sir, that the information you had was not reliable. You say -- I'm reading from it. It says: "The information I have is not reliable."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can put it that way. I said that it was second-hand information; those were my words. And I know that any such information is hardly reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you,,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I be curious why the witness says "second-hand information"? And before you said you heard people boasting to have been involved on the radio or on radio. What do you mean by "radio"? Is this broadcasting or is it a private radio connection, where you heard something by accident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in the police in Plaski, we had a radio set that could be set on the Ogulin police channel, the one that they used. The Ustasha side was referred to as Vujo, and the Chetnik side was referred to as Cedo. And this person was boasting about having stabbed to death this and that person, and this was for the purposes of intimidation. These were very ugly things that one could eavesdrop on, and I personally experienced them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, by the way, just to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually, if we could save that exhibit, please, and if it could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean the map with the circling of the Glibodol cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 19 of Exhibit 23 is admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The barracks at Licka Jesenica are at a higher elevation than Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to specify which part of Saborsko you have in mind. Saborsko stretches over 6 kilometres, and it is not on a higher ground than some parts of Saborsko. You have two mounts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Borik is one of them which may be on a -- more or less the same height.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of these two mounts? The interpreters didn't catch their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I spoke quickly. The hill called Borik is on the same level as the barracks, as well as Alan and Sivnik. These are all the mounts forming part of Mala Kapela range, and I believe that the upper part of Saborsko is even higher than the hill where the barracks are. And you can show me the map. I can point to those, and I believe they are on the same height above sea level, but I would need a map to be more precise in my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you testified about the -- about the church, the small church in Saborsko. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that small church was at a point that was lower in elevation than the Licka Jesenica barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that. If indeed there is a difference, it can't be that big, but you would have to show me the map to -- for me to be able to tell you precisely. I'm not sure. I don't think they're not on the same level, but I don't know which one is higher. Although the visibility is very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. From that point you can see -- you can see -- from that point you can see the Licka Jesenica barracks, and from Licka Jesenica barracks you can see the church; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the attack that you spoke about on the barracks of Licka Jesenica that occurred from the 5th of November to the 8th of November, that was -- that attack was repelled; it was not successful. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After three days of fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the 8th of November, it was defeated; it was not successful. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any certainty, but I think that it lasted until the 8th of November, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go -- let's talk about the attack itself on Saborsko on the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could go back to Exhibit 52, please. And if we could go to the first paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the first paragraph it's a -- I think the third -- no, sorry, the fourth sentence. It says -- no, sorry, it's the third sentence: "Furthermore, we have information that a part of hard-line Ustasha prepared, entrenched, and ready for a long-term battle. By direct reconnaissance and from the information given from the field, it was established that the enemy has not organised a classic defence but is fortifying using entrenched position with machine-guns," and it goes on. Now, that is consistent, that -- what's contained in there is consistent with what you observed, isn't it, because you testified on Monday that you observed that the people in Saborsko were "preparing seriously for defence." And you described the trenches that had been dug in Saborsko. So they had taken -- they had prepared defensive positions in Saborsko, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 3 of the B/C/S of this order and page 5 of the English. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to go to the rest room for a minute. I can really not go on at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a short break for ten minutes -- ten minutes or five minutes? We'll come back in five minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. --- Break taken at 4.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On this document if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page. And I'm looking at -- I want to look at 11(B) which is entitled "security," and it's on page 5 of the English at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it says: "All strangers moving towards the sector of unit deployment shall be kept and after interrogation removed, informing authorised officers thereof. Unknown persons who for any reason are found in the zone of troop deployment shall be arrested by the police authorities as for investigation and further action." Now, language like this was included in many or all of the orders regarding the attack on Saborsko; correct? This is standard language that was contained in the orders, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had -- the largest unit under my command was a company, but I suppose that this was the standard procedure, standard language used by the JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, the -- it's true, isn't it, that the military would not -- would never allow people who were not involved in the attack simply to show up in the area to do whatever they wanted, would it? Right? You agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can you please repeat your question. I was focussed on the text where it said "unknown persons." Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I suggest -- oh, I see, you were looking at the exhibit. I understand. Yes, I can repeat my question. The military, the JNA, would not -- would never or would never allow people who were not involved in the attack simply to show up in the area to do whatever they wanted, would it? It would never it allow that? It's part of standard military operations that you do not permit that, correct, which is why it appears in these orders?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that's the reason why, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there were no -- during the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, there were no -- nobody on your side, let's say, was killed, correct? From the TO, the police, or the JNA, there were no fighters who were killed. There was some injured, a couple who were injured, but nobody was killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The group that I led, we only had one slightly wounded person, and I know for a fact that nobody was killed in the other groups, although I don't know the exact number of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about your role in the attack. You testified that you started in -- you started off in Momcilovici village, that you attacked along the right flank, that at the beginning there was an air attack, that you engaged in hand-to-hand combat at a certain point and killed three enemy soldiers. You agree with me so far?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That at a certain point there was a danger of friendly fire and so you retreated to Vukelic Poljana; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I -- if it was interpreted as "friendly fire," I said fire from our barracks, and it wasn't -- it was the Vukelic Poljana and not something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I used the term "friendly fire" to mean fire from your own side. And I did try to say Vukelic Poljana like you did, but it may have come out differently. Now -- and then you testified that you did not enter Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us that Dusan Latas was part of your group; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could, I'd like to look at his account of the events, and it's Exhibit 605.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've seen this document before; we've talked about it. It's a report that was written on the 23rd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2, please, of both the English and the B/C/S. And if we could go to point 2 on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you see in that first paragraph he says -- he says: "The entire police unit," he's talking about the attack that was supposed to be on the 10th of November but it actually occurred on the 12th of November. And he says: "The unit was stationed in Momcilovici village," just like you said, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what part are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's point 2. It's the first paragraph of point 2, which is halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My point 2 doesn't say: "The entire police unit." It says: "The general attack on Saborsko."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sorry, I'm reading from the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second sentence: "However, the weather was very bad."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the third sentence. I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The third sentence says that: "Those two days the entire police" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "The entire police unit was stationed in Momcilovici village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. "Stationed in Momcilovici village."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have been more clear. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just like you said, "started off in Momcilovici village," right? That's what you said, too, that your --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph -- it says: "On the 12th November, 1991, following the air attack," so there was -- it started with an air attack just like you said, right? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then he says: "The police unit and the special unit made up the right flank of our attack," just like you said, went on the right flank. Correct? Do you see that? It's also on the second paragraph, it's the third sentence of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please read out the villages mentioned there, because it says the village of Strkovi, Brdine and Alan grid reference. You actually skipped two lines and then mentioned the right flank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I'm skipping over that. I'm just going to the sentence where he says: "The police unit and the special unit made up the right flank of our attack." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's just like you said, you were on the right flank; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then skip the next sentence. And -- and then he says: "At one point we simply mingled with 10 or 13 MUP members which resulted in a show-down with knives and hand-grenades. The police acted especially well in that situation as they inflicted great casualties on the MUP in a very brief time." Now, that's consistent with what you said that you engaged in hand-to-hand combat and three MUP Croatian -- MUP men were killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This hand-to-hand combat is a bit too strong of a word. It was close combat. And it's true that we mingled with the policemen, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and stay on page 2 of the English and go to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You'll see that he says that -- and it's at the bottom -- end of the -- bottom of the page in English, and I think it's at the top of the page in the B/C/S here, that -- it's a paragraph that begins: "At that moment, a line of our tanks was supposed to stretch in front of us, so we lay down and waited for the tanks." And then he says: "We thought it would be best if we retreated to the fall-back position, Vukelic Poljana village." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive the translation. I only received the translation up to the word "tanks."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let me repeat it. Are you receiving translation now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: All right. Do you see the sentence where he says: "We thought it would be best if we retreated to the fall-back position, Vukelic Poljana village." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's also what you -- what you said happened, that you retreated to Vukelic Poljana village; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we turn to the next page in the English, please, and stay on this page of the B/C/S. And scroll down a little bit more on the B/C/S. There. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in the end of the paragraph -- you see there's a paragraph right before point 3. Go to the end of the paragraph before that. He says -- he's speaking about being in Vukelic Poljana village. "We left scouts and snipers at the advance points." And then he says: "We established communication with our staff and we were ordered to move towards Saborski along the main road. We could see that Saborski was on fire and that it was no longer there." Now, that part of the account is different from what you told us, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, significantly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, what Mr. Latas says happened is exactly what happened. You went towards Saborski, you were ordered to go to Saborsko, you went there, towards there, you saw that it was on fire and that it was no longer there; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I explained where I found the first group of civilians at the crossroads, along the road leading to Vukelic Poljana, on the asphalt road, and I was quite specific in describing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you deny, sir, that you were ordered to go back to Saborsko -- go towards Saborsko, that you went towards Saborsko, that you saw that it was on fire and that it was no longer there. You deny that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point where I stood, one could see the reflection of fire. We couldn't see what was on fire, but we could see that the fire was burning. It was already getting dark because it was winter-time, it was late in the afternoon. As for what Dusan Latas saw, you should ask him. Nobody was in the position to order me anything because I didn't have any radio communication. My radio set had broken down, and I ordered my men to withdraw on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well -- so when Dusan Latas says: "We established communication with our staff and were ordered to move towards Saborsko," you deny that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny that that occurred for the reason that I didn't establish communication with anyone until we came to Plavca Draga, which is about 15 kilometres away. And it was only then when we reached the battalion command that we found other people and discussed the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, Dusan Latas says that you could -- that he could see and -- that Saborsko was no longer there. And that was actually the aim of the attack, wasn't it, to make sure that Saborsko would no longer be there, right? Wasn't that the aim of the attack, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't the one designating the goals of the attack; I was just in command of a company. And I completed my mission to the best of my abilities. I can't answer your question. The person who issued the order for attack was the one who specified the goal of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the order for the attack? What were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To crush the Ustasha stronghold, to free the road, and to lift the siege of the barracks in Plaski -- rather, in Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said crush the Ustasha stronghold in Saborsko. I think that's what it said verbatim in my order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that was the objective of the attack, to crush the Ustasha stronghold in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it said there. Maybe I got a word wrong, but I think that that's exactly what it said verbatim, plus liberate or free the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the day after the attack you visited some civilians who were taken to a school in Licka Jesenica, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the Serb who had taken him -- taken them there? I think you gave us the last name, Solaja.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I met that group of people at the junction of roads. There is a road there leading to Vukelic Poljana. This is below Borik towards Licka Jesenica. I could see there that one of our TO members with a rifle on his shoulder, he was quite short and I think his name was Sreta or Sveta, he accompanied that group of people. There was a youngish man among them. I didn't recognise him right away, but when I came closer I could see it was Solaja. I don't remember his first name. I know, however, that he was a Serb living in Saborsko. I didn't know the other people personally. And then another Solaja came down from forest yelling: Solaja, Solaja. He wasn't with that group but he came out saying: Solaja, Solaja so that nobody would fire at him and he came straight at me at that junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why would nobody fire at him if he said: Solaja, Solaja?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely in his head that meant that he would be safe because everybody in Licka Jesenica knew that Solaja was a Serb last name. This was a younger person, a civilian. And at that time anybody who came out of the forest was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you first, how do you spell this Solaja typically in Serb, in Latin letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a letter in Serbian language, "sh." So the first letter is S-o-l-a-j-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were talking about your visit to the school in Licka Jesenica on the day after the attack on Saborsko, so on the 13th of November, 1991, where you saw civilians. Now, in fact, sir, when you saw those civilians there, you cursed their Ustasha mothers, you asked them where their sons were, and you told them that you would send them to Ogulin to Rudi Spehar to tell him that Saborsko did not exist anymore. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that is true, sir. Whoever knows me, even a little bit, will know full well that I never communicated in that way, especially not with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at exhibit -- sorry, it's not an exhibit, a document 01510812.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a statement, sir, that was given by Slavko Dumencic on the 25th of January, 1992, in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could go, please, to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. And he's talking about -- well, I'm sorry, I think I rushed this a little bit. If we could go to page 1, please, on both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You see he's talking about Saborsko on the 12th of November, and he talks about being with his family in the basement of the house of his neighbour Stevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Stevo Solaja, which is the family that you had told us about before. And he says: "As the occupying army began to enter Saborsko in the afternoon that day, the inhabitants were leaving their houses and fleeing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the next-to-last sentence on the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to the next page on both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He says that they went to a school in Licka Jesenica. And then it says: "Nikola Medakovic met us there and insulted us, cursed our Ustasha mothers and asked us where our sons were. He also yelled that he would send us to Ogulin to Rudi Spehar to tell us that Saborsko did not exist anymore." And that happened, didn't it, sir, you did that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen. One can clearly see that the person giving the statement was instructed as to what to say. I met them at the junction of the roads from Licka Jesenica to Saborsko and Vukelic Poljana, which is 1 kilometre away from the school. I never cursed anyone's Ustasha mother, nor did I ask them where their sons were. As for sending a letter to Rudo Spehar, I said clearly when asked by Mr. Milovancevic. Someone gave this statement under instructions in order to place me somewhere where I wasn't. I didn't get to the school until the following day. I came in civilian clothes, I had a track-suit on, and I had no weapons on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just find out something. On what basis do you say one can see that the person who wrote the statement was instructed to write -- to write it this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it says here that I told them to go to Rudi Spehar. I gave a letter to one of the civilians in an envelope marked for Rudo Spehar. There was no way they could know what was written in that letter. And there are some portions of the letter quoted here, which means that somebody read this letter to them and told them what to say to incriminate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are the parts that are quoted from the letter in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian version, this is behind the words "Medakovic Nikola," where it says: "Insulting us and cursing our Ustasha mothers, asking where our sons were." And then it says: "He said he yelled that he would send us to Ogulin to Rudi Spehar to tell him that Saborsko is no more and that Ogulin was under threat as well." Most likely the Prosecutor will be using that letter that I wrote and we should be able to compare the two texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying -- let me understand you. Are you saying the sentence starting: "He also yelled that he would send us to Ogulin to Rudi Spehar to tell him that Saborsko did not exist anymore and that he also threatened Ogulin," you're saying that's also a quotation from the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something along those lines is written in the letter, namely that Saborsko is no more. And I warned the Croatian authorities in Ogulin -- I think they have the letter here, so we should put it on the ELMO so that I don't have to paraphrase my own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, we understand that -- I just want to know what is it that was quoted from the letter. You're saying: "He also yelled that he would send us to Ogulin to Rudi Spehar to tell him that Saborsko did not exist anymore and that he also threatened Ogulin." That is a quotation from your letter. Is that your letter, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my letter it says that Saborsko, unfortunately, is no more and that it most likely will never exist again. And then there is a sentence about Ogulin, and we can discuss that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Ogulin is mentioned twice there. And what you have just told us is not what is written here, so that's not a quotation from your letter, sir. But anyway, thank you so much. Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, the truth is, isn't it, sir, that that was something that you were saying -- you were saying and writing in those days, that you were taunting Croats with the fact that Saborsko no longer existed. Isn't that true, sir? And you said it to this man and that group of civilians and you wrote it to Rudolf Spehar. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I met that group of civilians under the circumstances that I described to you. The next time I saw them was when I entered the school in Licka Jesenica in civilian clothes, asking them whether they needed anything, whether anybody was threatening them, and whether they wanted to go to the Croatian side. I never yelled, especially not then. I expressed my force only in relation to people who were my equals. That's my principle. Everything else is invented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just warn you once again, please listen to the questions and answer directly to the questions. Three-quarters of what you've just told us has nothing to do with the question that was put to you. The question to you had been: You said it to this man and that group of civilians and you wrote it to Rudolf Spehar. Isn't that true? The answer should be: Yes, it is true; or no it is not true. Simple. We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you're right. I do have the letter, and I'm -- let's look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 269 and it's in evidence. If we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You recognise this letter, sir? Do you need to see the next page?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could you scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is no next page, it's just down at the bottom. Is that your signature on this letter, sir, your name, your signature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now, just a moment ago when you were quoting the letter you said -- you quoted the letter as saying -- it's at line 10 -- 11 of 65 of the transcript today. It says: "In my letter it says that Saborsko, unfortunately, is no more and that it most likely will never exist again."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look -- scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say -- the sentence actually reads: "Now there is no Saborsko anymore and it is likely that it never -- it will never be there again." I don't see the word "unfortunately."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mistake. I fully accept that. And at the beginning of the letter I said "following grave events."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And you say that Saborsko suffered the same sad fate of Vaganac, Dreznik, Lovinac and all other places whose residents tried to defy the Serbs by using force. And you say that: "The immediate cause for the attack were your soldiers' gruesome actions towards our civilians during the attack on Licka Jesenica." And then you talk about: "Those who chop live people into pieces and castrate them, those who cut off their ears and pick their eyes cannot hope for anything better." Now, that's a reference, isn't it, to the three men who were killed at Glibodol cross; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a reference to Vukelic, Branko, called Sapina, and Vukelic Javor, who were also victims at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. But, sir, those people were not chopped and had their ears cut off and castrated. That's a specific reference to the three men who were killed at Glibodol cross. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these words, cuts into pieces, castrates, cuts off ears and picks eyes, the reference is precisely to the three men. An atrocity is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The three men at Glibodol cross, just so we're clear; correct. The three men killed at Glibodol cross?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, in fact, that was not the immediate cause for the attack on Saborsko, was it, because the decision to attack Saborsko was made before that happened, right? So what you wrote in this letter was not true.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're coming to the essence of what you tried to use to entrap me. It was only yesterday or before yesterday that I found out that the attack was being ordered earlier on. At the time when I was drafting this letter was after the Glibodol Kriz -- it was after the Glibodol Kriz events that I received order for attack. And Colonel Cedomir Bulat stated that such events would not be allowed to happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that -- all what you're saying notwithstanding. The fact of the matter is that the order was made at the very latest on the 7th and it is mailed out on the 8th. So that death could not have been the immediate cause of the attack. You were not the person who was ordering the attack; the attack was ordered by your seniors. You've told us so just before the break. Isn't that correct? Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, and I received the order after these events at Glibodol Kriz --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the point. That's not -- you may have received -- whenever you received the order, you may have received it whenever you received it. However, the person who wrote that order on the 7th, who decided on the attack, did so before the death at Glibodol cross. The Prosecutor is not saying that you knew then in 1991, before the deaths of these three that -- the immediate cause of the attack. He's saying the truth of the matter is that the immediate cause of the attack was not the death of the three, because the attack was -- the decision to attack was made before they died. It's a simple thing. We've talked about it a little earlier today. We don't have to waste any more time on it. I asked you a question on it, I insisted you answer it, you agreed with me. And if you will listen to the questions put to you, very attentively, you would not waste this time by telling us about your writing of the letter which was -- has nothing to do with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In some of the answers to questions today, sir, you have expressed some reluctance in trying to say what the goals of the attack were, but how is it that you were so confident since you did not order the attack on Saborsko, that wasn't your decision, how is it on the 13th of November you felt confident to tell -- to write in this letter what the cause of the attack was, since you had not ordered it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in terms of the contents themselves, they are being distorted. What is the immediate cause; that is a factual question. What is the goal behind an order for an attack? What is the goal behind the order of the Tactical Group 2 or that of the 5th Army District command? And this is a very dangerous way of replacing the thesis and of distorting the order in which all of these orders were issued. If the 5th Military District of the JNA, through the Secretariat for National Defence, issued the decision to establish Tactical Group 2 and the 13th Corps issued an order for an attack that was carried out by the Tactical Group 2, then that is where the goals are contained. The witness here is being asked about a letter which was written after all these events and which has to do with Glibodolski Kriz, but this letter has nothing to do with the order for the attack against Saborsko, which is a military operation involving the air force, tanks, and so on and so forth. And the witness here is being asked whether what is contained in this letter is the immediate cause of the attack. I believe that we are misconstruing matters here. We are lumping together matters that are significant and insignificant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at no point in time did the witness hesitate in talking about the purpose of the order for an attack. The order for an attack is something that is issued by the military command. He interpreted it. The evidence was led, and we know precisely when the orders were issued. The events at Glibodolski Kriz are being tied up with the reason behind the military operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, have you read this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you read the paragraph where the author of this letter says: "The immediate cause for the attack were your soldiers' gruesome actions towards our civilians during the attack on Licka Jesenica. Those who chopped live people into pieces and castrated them, those who cut off their ears and picked their eyes out cannot hope for anything better." That's -- what the Prosecutor is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. But this has nothing to do with the order for the attack, and that is the personal view of the witness here. Now, what an order for an attack is and what the reasons behind the order were, which were entertained by the 13th Corps, by Tactical Group 2, the 5th Military District, that's quite a different matter because the military orders and actions one matter. Now, the events touched upon in this letter by the witness on the ground are quite a different matter. We cannot tie the orders issued by military commands in with the letter that was written by a person who took part in the fighting on the ground, and that is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that there is a distinction between the cause of the attack and the aim of the attack. And the point I was trying to make is that when I asked the witness earlier today, it's at page 59, about the aim of the attack, he said: Well, I can't tell you what the aim of the attack was because that was made above me. And I was trying to draw a parallel that the similar -- you would think there would be a similar answer with respect to what the cause of the attack was, also something known to the people who ordered the attack. And so I'm asking him why it is that he is able to write on the 13th of November what the cause of the attack is when he was here reluctant to testify about the aim of the attack because it's something made above his grade, it's made above him by superiors. Now, it's a parallel, but I of course accept that there is a distinction between the cause of the attack and the aim of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not a parallel. In our view, this is a dangerous attempt at changing the content and the sense of what is contained is there. We saw three documents, orders, the order for the setting up of Tactical Group 2, of the 5th military command, we have the 13th Corps order, and then the order issued by the commander of Tactical Group 2. And all of them talk of the goals and the purpose of the military action to be carried out by the military forces. Now, the witness here talks merely about one detail. My learned friend Prosecutor put a line of questions to him; isn't it true that the Croatian forces have been attacking the JNA barracks from the 5th to the 8th, and the answers he received were in the affirmative. And the Prosecutor confirmed through the witness the contents of these orders. And now through this letter written by the president of the Plaski and Ogulin municipality, he is trying to depict as the role and the aim of the attack something that is quite different. And this is what I wanted to draw the Bench's attention to. As my learned friend said himself, there is a distinction there. The Prosecutor can now ask the witness what he had in mind whilst drafting the letter, but it wasn't the witness who set the goal of the attack through this letter. He tied up the military operation with the events at Glibodolski Kriz, also with those events. But that's as far as this went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put the question a little differently to you. How did you know on the 13th of November, 1991, what the cause, the immediate cause, of the attack was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this letter was written 15 years ago. I was 24 years old at the time, and I was deeply shaken by what the Ustasha soldier did to our people. One of the men was a fighter of mine. In addition to that, I was dissatisfied with the way the operation at Saborsko ended. Thirdly, you have to bear in mind my social background. You have to know that Saborsko is very similar to the area I hailed from, where I lived, and I can understand these people. And it wasn't that I was happy with anybody's distress. I was writing this to a very cool-minded HDZ member who I had negotiated with on several occasions and who threatened me with throwing me in a jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can I -- I'm going to interrupt you because you've gone on for a long time but you haven't answered my question. How did you know or why did you think you knew on the 13th of November, 1991, what the immediate cause of the attack was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Couldn't we first make one thing clear. Witness, was this, what you wrote there, your personal view or was it an attempt to describe the reality, the real cause? It could have been just your interpretation also. Therefore, your question sounds as if he knew that. Then we can ask how did he know. But maybe in a different approach in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if maybe I could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to answer His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was presenting my personal view at the time only. I was in a very difficult psychological state of mind. I saw that the people who were not to blame were the ones who suffered; whereas the perpetrators of the events at Saborsko, which the Prosecutor asked me about, were still at large. Therefore, this was my personal view, Your Honour, that I presented here. The units I commanded over were never bigger than --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a personal letter, is it? It's a letter written in your capacity as president of the Plaski municipality. This is an official letter, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: With a political nature --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, does the president of any municipality command over any military units? Do you know of such an instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you have written here "SAO Krajina" at the top, "Plaski Municipal Assembly president," and you have signed the letter and stamped it with an official seal. This is an official letter to Rudolf Spehar who himself was the president of the Ogulin municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the bottom of the B/C/S version of the letter, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: All the way to the bottom I think, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an official letter, isn't it, sir? This is not a personal letter.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the official letter from the president of the municipality of Plaski to the president of the municipality of Ogulin. It was never the subject of discussion of the Municipal Assembly of Plaski or the Executive Council. I wrote it and my secretary typed it out, and I stand by every word written in that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, this letter is not a regretful or a sad letter at all; it's a taunting letter, isn't it? You say: "Now there is no Saborsko anymore and it is likely that it will never be there again. May this be a warning to all those who are planning to impose their power on the Serbs by using force." You weren't upset about what happened in Saborsko. You were happy about what happened there and wanted it to be a warning to others. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're picking out parts of the letter that you want to serve your turn. Why don't you go back to the beginning of the letter where I stated in line 3 "Saborsko befell a sad" -- "A sad fate befell Saborsko," and as I mentioned here, Saborsko -- and then I mentioned all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The last -- sir, at the beginning of the cross-examination I asked you if there was any justification for the crimes that occurred in Saborsko, and you said: No, there's no justification for crimes. And isn't the last sentence of this letter and the -- this letter in its entirety, the last sentence which reads: "There is no evil in doing evil to evil people," isn't that a justification of the crimes that occurred in Saborsko? Aren't you trying to justify it there in that letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're a lawyer. This is the short definition of necessity, and if you as a lawyer take necessity into account, then this is a mitigating circumstance. Because you're trying to ward off greater evil, although in the end we suffered that evil four years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you think that necessity justified crimes, the crimes that occurred in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, on that day I didn't know that those crimes had occurred because I had not been in Saborsko yet by then. I thought that all civilians had left Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that that was how the operation ended. This is what I thought at the time I wrote this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you answer my question, please? Do you think that necessity justifies or justified the crimes that occurred in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, sir. Perhaps you haven't understood me clearly. I thought that this was a pure operation, faultless operation, and that nothing had happened to civilians. And of course whenever you have a person killed, that is a misfortune in itself. Even when you see cattle slaughtered. I wrote this letter in this confused state of mind, but I do stand by it because it reflects what was my position and my opinion at the time. I wasn't pleased with seeing other people's houses on fire. Those were the evils that I referred to. I did not know at the time about the tragedy that had happened in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, but if you stand by it at this point in time, then there's no need for you to refer us to the confusion that you suffered at the time you wrote it because you still believe it. You are not confused now. You are not a 24-year-old youngster, you are a 39-year-old mature man and you still stand by it. So save us the time and don't refer us to your confusion. If you were saying you are holding a different view today from what you wrote here, I would think you would be justified in telling us about your confusion, but if you still stand by it then there's no need to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how it was interpreted to you, but that's the gist of what I stated. I state that this letter is credible, that I signed it, and that this was my opinion at the time. Of course, with hindsight I can be cleverer than I was then, but it is of no use to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you would then be: Do you stand by the letter, or do you regret some of the things you wrote in the letter, or do you have a changed to mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do regret some formulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you are justified in saying what you are saying. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when you testified at the very end of your direct examination about this letter and -- and you told Mr. Milovancevic about having written this letter, why didn't you tell us then that you regretted writing it, or that you regretted some formulations in it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked here to answer the questions, and I was warned that, in fact, by His Honour on several occasions. And Mr. Milovancevic didn't ask me anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I notice that the LiveNote is down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Not the LiveNote, but the e-court --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's right, the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm happy to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would think we don't have to go into that why regretting only today not the day before yesterday or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say do not go into it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yeah, just go on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I'm happy to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're lucky, Your Honour. Oh, I've got mine now -- no, I don't. Your Honour, would you like me to proceed or wait to get this fixed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you were that young man of 24, was your conduct and your action and your views, was it -- were these things coloured by what had happened to your forebears in your opinion at the hands of the Ustashas? Because you still seem to feel pretty strongly. I'm trying to put myself in the mind of that 24-year-old who had to make those decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at one point when Mr. Milovancevic was examining me, I said that the crossroads or the turning point in my life was the event at Glibodolski Kriz. What I saw with my own eyes there caused enormous problems to me. You see, when you're 24 and when you're entrusted with commanding over a unit and when you have to take a person out of their home and then return their bodies back, then this is a problem to me and these families. I knew all these fighters and their families personally. They had been living there for hundreds of years. It wasn't a group of mercenaries that I had under my command that I could use whichever way I wanted. To this day, I have been experiencing the consequences of the conflict. Now, as for my ancestors, well, perhaps I would have been a different person had my grandfather lived to see the day when I was born rather than having to not even know where his grave was because he had been killed by the Ustasha in World War II and his body was buried and cemented somewhere. However, I went to school together with Croats. There were Croats in Plaski as well. The secretary of the Executive Council, of which I was the president, was a Croat, a lady Croat. I don't have trouble communicating with Croats, but I do have trouble communicating with the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But can you make a distinction in your mind? When the chips are down, are you really able to make that distinction? Were you able to make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in addition to Saborsko, the part of Plaski toward Ogulin there were the villages of Turkalji and Vajin Vrh that were inhabited by Croats. I went to their homes where they would even invite me to share their festivities on Christmas. One of the ladies there gave birth to her child and she was put up in the same room as my wife. And these were people who had not been instrumentalised by others, as were those unfortunate people in Saborsko. When the international monitors came to Plaski, they came up with a list of names of 67 Croats and non-Serbs from Plaski. The first question they put to me was where these people were. I told them that some of them were still there and that some of them were put up at my home. As I said the secretary, Nedeljka Trbojevic, nee Sucic, was a Croat and her family spent the entire war at my home. I didn't have any problems there. They asked me why had those events at Saborsko transpired. I told them: Well, I'm sure in your homes -- back at home you also see people who are merciless and who commit crimes, and the same type of crimes were committed by some people in Saborsko, crimes that caused consternation on the part of the international community. And this is my opinion today. In order to obtain a state of their own, they had to sacrifice half of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So do you think that the end always justifies the means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean wartime goals? If the goal is to save an entire settlement, if the goal is to enable people to lead normal lives, if an -- and if in order to achieve that you have to do some ugly things because you have to liberate that settlement, you have to lift the siege. I think that all our armies, when they receive orders, have to take that into account. If the order is to lift the siege, all I could do was try to save the lives of people under my command and to preserve my honour. And I affirm that I did that. I preserve my honour. I never fired at anyone who was helpless or unarmed, nor did I ever order anyone to do that. And whoever did that needs to be tried, either before this court or before some other court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Medakovic. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I do want to stay with this letter just for one more moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier that then and even today you did not know who was responsible for the murder of those three men at Glibodol cross, and you couldn't -- you couldn't even say that they came from Saborsko. So how -- how is it that the people of Saborsko -- even in your mind then, on the 13th of November, how is it that you could think that the people of Saborsko could be responsible for that and be held responsible and suffer evil in the attack because of it? How could you think that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, sir, that they boasted themselves on radio frequency. When someone says: That man of yours, he screamed really loudly as we stabbed him with the knife, he's doing that in order to hurt you. And it was I who talked that man into joining the unit, who mobilised him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because you also told us you thought that information was unreliable and you told us that it came over the radio from Ogulin. Did you -- did you think, sir, that the entire village of Saborsko should suffer and be destroyed because of what had happened to those three men? Even though you have no -- no reliable evidence that the -- that it had happened as a result of anybody in Saborsko? Did you think that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, sir. You are misconstruing it. I said that everybody individually has to be held accountable for crimes. And as for everything together which took place in Saborsko, I wasn't the one who decided on that. I described to you exactly in which combat I took place, under what circumstances, and who was killed then. And now you're trying to shift to my shoulders --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to talk about what you wrote. And what you wrote on the 13th of November, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are trying to talk about what the witness wrote as saying -- but this trying seems to be a little difficult for the witness and I would have reacted before already. Your question, in fact, was compound. It was, on the one hand, assuming that the witness had no reason to think that the people of Saborsko were responsible; and on the other hand, we should have said: Given he was convinced it was somebody from Saborsko, was that a justification or a good reason for a fight against the village. You should separate these two things a little bit. And I would like to ask the one thing myself to the witness. Were you at that time, on the 13th of -- yeah, on the 13th, still convinced -- or were you sort of convinced based on this, as you now say, unreliable radio frequency notion that -- that it was people from Saborsko? Was that your conviction at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, as I was writing this letter, it was my firm conviction that this was a show produced together by the forces from Saborsko and Ogulin because that's precisely where they met up and went into further operation. These unfortunate people had come from Dabar, where they were on some civilian business, having collected the horses and transporting them in a trailer. It was my firm conviction then, and I put in a lot of effort to find out that perpetrators were even paid to receive information because I wanted to know who was that monster who could have done it. It was my firm conviction that they did it together and that they drew satisfaction as they tortured these people for several hours. They did it together because this is a junction of roads in the forest and there is a clearing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is to be pre-supposed to the next question. Please, Mr. Whiting, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's assume -- let's assume what you say -- how you felt at the time and what you believed at the time. Is that -- is that a justification for what occurred in Saborsko, the attack on Saborsko and the crimes that were committed in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No crime can ever justify another crime. Innocent people always become victims. Had I found those people in the act, had I caught them in the act, they would not have lived to stand trial. I can tell you about my feelings, and now that I'm 40 years old I can tell you that violence begets more violence, and that it is up to the Judges to solve these issues, not up to revengeful people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, isn't it also up to commanders and leaders such as yourself as the president of the Plaski municipality and commander of 60 men in this operation, isn't it up to people like you, commanders, to not give in to passions and speculations and myths and to -- and to follow the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend has no foundation for putting this question because the witness never stated anything of this sort earlier to justify this question. On the contrary, the witness said something quite opposite; namely, that no crime justifies another crime. I don't see why we are wasting time now on such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, first of all, that the letter that we have before us does seek to justify what happened, the evil that happened in Saborsko. It says: "There is no evil in doing evil to evil people." And secondly, I was just asking my question going on what the witness said, which is: "Violence begets more violence and it is up to the Judges" -- sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just keep quiet. You'll be addressed and you will be given an opportunity to answer. Right now the lawyers are speaking to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "That it is up to the Judges to solve these issues," and I was just going on from there that -- to ask him if he believed that also commanders and leaders had a responsibility during wartime to follow the law and not succumb to passions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any reply to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but the witness stated that at the time when he was writing the letter he didn't know about the victims, he hadn't been in the village at that point, that he didn't know about the destruction and the suffering. Why is this question put to him as, then, though he knew all that? That was the point of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I won't allow you to speak because I don't think the last reply addresses the question, and I'm just ruling the objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in fact you did -- when you wrote this letter, you did know that evil had been done in Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, didn't you? And that's why you wrote "there is no evil in doing evil to evil people."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that I didn't know of the extent of what had happened. I told you that given my background I consider it an evil event when somebody's house is set on fire. We refer to the cattle as treasure in my region. When we see cattle wandering off, we know that that's evil, that that's misfortune, and it bothers me. As for the extent of destruction and civilian deaths, I learned of that only when the sanitization of the terrain was conducted. That's when I learned of that. Nobody has a right to commit a crime on my behalf. And to answer your question about the leaders and commanders, let me tell you that in Iraq, British and American forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not letting me speak --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put that question to me, but you can't put the same question to the US president. You should have the same position to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, the US president is not in this court to answer any questions. You're not dealing with Iraqi issues. We're dealing with the Croatian issues or the former Yugoslavian issues. I'll ask you to refrain from referring us to the president of the United States or to Iraq. Let's deal with the facts that are before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, everybody knew by the 13th of November, 1991, the day after, that Saborsko was no more. As you wrote it, "There is no Saborsko anymore," that it had been destroyed, that the people had left, and hat civilians had been killed. Everybody knew that, including you. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, sir. That is not true. There was no television, no cameras to record that at the time. That's a huge area. The village itself is 6 to 8 kilometres long. We had no fuel. We had no resources. I did not have a helicopter to conduct a reconnaissance above Saborsko. I wasn't even there --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you wrote that Saborsko is -- "there is no Saborsko anymore." Those are your words. So you knew on the 13th of November when you wrote this letter that there was no Saborsko anymore, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no more as an Ustasha stronghold. There was no resistance there any longer. It simply didn't exist. There was nobody there to do things that had been done before by people to whom I refer as Ustashas. There were no longer such people in Saborsko. And let me tell you, they were the first ones to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, and you were a 24-year-old man, but you were -- you were president of the municipality, you were commander in the operation, you had been the -- you had been and you were still in command of the special unit of the SAO Krajina police. Those are all important positions of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true that I was the commander of the operation. It's not true that I was at the helm of the special unit. Sir, once again you are misquoting facts, and then you want me to give my position. I cannot do that when the facts are incorrect. It is not true, and I disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir -- well, I think there may have been a misinterpretation. I didn't mean to suggest you were the commander of the operation. Let me put it differently. You held important positions of responsibility at that time, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a very important post, one and only, and it was called president of municipality during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is not the letter of -- well, I'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to leave this letter unless there is other questions from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on from this letter unless there are other questions from Your Honours about the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have one question about the letter. What is it, sir, that you regret today in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I regret writing the letter at the time while the situation was not entirely clear to me as to what had truly happened. Second, I regret because I myself experienced the fate of those unfortunate people in Saborsko. I experienced that in 1995. Had I had that experience, I would have never allowed the people leaving their homes to take the letter with them. It was humiliating enough to leave their homes, and they didn't need additional humiliation of serving as my couriers. As for Rudo Spehar and Croatian authorities and everything else I felt at the time, I still have those feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate what you have told us. There's only one point in all the points that you've given us that has a direct relation to the contents of the letter, namely writing the letter when you are not clear of the facts. What facts were you not clear about at the time you wrote the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know the extent of civilian casualties and destruction in Saborsko. I'm stating that with full responsibility here under oath. I didn't know of deaths of civilians. I knew that their soldiers were killed and that houses were set on fire. It's an evil event whenever somebody's child is killed, regardless of whose army they are members of. But I didn't know of the extent of the destruction in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you knew that there are soldiers who were killed and that they are children of some people, those soldiers that were killed? That you didn't regret -- that you do not regret? Do I understand you to be saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I took part in combat. They fired at me. I fired at them at close range. I was the first one leading the column. I took part in it. By some luck I survived and they didn't. That's war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But you don't regret that their soldiers died. I'll tell you why I'm asking the question. You say -- you said in your answer: "I knew that their soldiers were killed and that houses were set on fire." And then you go on to say: "It's an evil event whenever somebody's child is killed, regardless of whose army they are members of." Now, what you seem to be saying to us is that you regret if civilians die, you regret the fact that their houses were burnt, but you don't regret that their soldiers died, but in the same breath you say: If a soldier dies, irrespective of which army he belongs to, it is still an evil thing. I am not quite sure I understand you, and I would like you to clarify this. Because I would really like to understand what it is that you do regret in this letter. What are you saying? I find some kind of equivocation in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will give you a completely frank answer. The soldiers, the enemy soldiers, the Ustashas who died in the conflict with us were very young. I could see them myself. They were young men, and I felt great sorrow that such young children were there. I was 24 myself, and they were younger than me. The other thing I wanted to say, I read once a book, Hemingway's book, which in the preface says that the death of each man reduces my being as well. This is something that one learns as one grows older. How I regret that those Croatian soldiers died, but at the time I felt proud that I was able to neutralise them. I never bragged about this in bars or anywhere else. I never talked about these events before coming here to the Tribunal. I never wrote books, and a lot of people wrote books even though they never saw action. They are trying to portray things as it suits them. I am telling you about what I experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not go much further. Is there anything else other than what you've told us that you regret in the letter, in the contents of the letter? Not sending people as couriers or writing to the addressee, but in the content of the letter is there anything that -- other than what you have told us that you regret today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll down on my monitor? Yes. Thank you.
