I think that this line here: "May this be a warning to all those who thought that they could impose their power by force over Serbian people," it was no warning to them, the fate that the misfortunate people in Saborsko suffered; they used it to their own advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive interpretation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So sorry. Who used it to their own advantage and what is it they used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a peaceful village, Saborsko was turned into a stronghold when people from elsewhere were brought. You were able to see yourselves that Muslims were brought there. Non-Catholics were brought to a Catholic area to have people under their command there. Nothing is sacred to those people. They sacrificed them deliberately because they knew that that would draw a response from the JNA. They needed human victims in order to attract the pity of Europe. Tudjman was their leader, and he stated that he knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you. My -- what I would like to find out from you -- and if you don't have anything else, just tell me you don't have anything else. My question to you simply is: What is it in this letter that you regret? Now, you've told us you regret the statement that "let this be a warning." Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I regret writing that "it is not evil to do evil to evil people," I regret ever doing evil to anyone. I was frequently forced, placed between a rock and a hard place, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that all you regret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, Mr. -- Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to take too much of your time, but I would like to ask you also about that. This sentence in the end sort of summarising the message you wanted to give at that time, was this an expression saying at that time you learned somewhere, not exactly defining a justification, but this is a moral message, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've noticed throughout my testimony that I like to use sayings that are traditional. I don't know how well they translate into English, but where I come from we have sayings that are over 100 years old and that have quite a lot of meaning to us. I'm sure that they are difficult to translate into your language. I think that this phrase is mentioned here somewhere, you know the sayings "tit for tat," but in a different sense. I was not the one who coined this saying. I just used it at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is what I was thinking, that you -- it caught you in this moment and you had the feeling that this would be a good summary idea, that it would catch what you wanted to say in this letter at that time. And could it be that you are regretting the contents also due to this strong language you used in the light of what you know now what were really the unhappy events in Saborsko? You were referring to unhappy events in Saborsko; this is a foggy expression. It seems to cover what we know or you know today about the crimes, but at that time it was just a strong language, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is also significant is to whom this letter is addressed. I sent this letter to Rudolf Spehar who at that time in my mind represented the Croatian side, the face of the Croatian side that I was familiar with. I talked to him after writing this letter. Perhaps I wrote this deliberately in such strong terms so that he could understand that we are prepared to fight, to fight to the last man, if necessary, but we were not ready to accept him and what he represented in my mind. I talked to him when UNPROFOR arrived in 1992 or in 1993. This was in Vojnovic. And he never once asked he about this letter, and I kept repeating what is stated at the end of this letter: Give us the books that we need, give us what we had created together so that we can negotiate the border. At the time I believed that the Republic of Serbian Krajina would continue to exist. It is very difficult for me now to justify my acts. I'm not under indictment here. If somebody should issue an indictment against me, I would gladly respond. I would gladly respond to any prosecutor except for the prosecutor in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. Okay. We'll take an adjournment for the day, and the matter will -- stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the same courtroom, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
